nameStory: Common Kidney-Vetch gets its unusual name from the kidney-shaped leaflets that make up its compound leaves. The 'vetch' part comes from its membership in the legume family, though it's not a true vetch. Its scientific name 'vulneraria' means 'wound healer,' reflecting its long history as a medicinal plant in European folk medicine.
description: Common Kidney-Vetch is a low-growing perennial herb with distinctive clusters of bright yellow flowers that bloom in dense, rounded heads. This European native typically grows 6-18 inches tall with a spreading habit. Its most notable features are its silvery-green compound leaves and cheerful yellow flower clusters that sit atop sturdy stems. As a member of the legume family, it's related to beans, peas, and clovers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers packed tightly into rounded, cushion-like clusters about an inch across. Each tiny flower has the classic pea-family shape with a banner petal on top. The flower heads feel dense and slightly fuzzy when touched gently.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 3-15 small, kidney-shaped leaflets arranged along a central stem. The leaves have a distinctive silvery-green color with a soft, velvety texture due to fine hairs covering the surface.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats or cushions rarely exceeding 18 inches tall. Stems are often somewhat woody at the base and can feel slightly rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, inflated pods typical of legumes that contain 1-2 seeds. The pods are initially green and papery, turning brown as they mature and making a soft rustling sound when dry.

habitat: In New England, Common Kidney-Vetch is extremely rare, found occasionally in coastal areas, particularly on sandy soils, rocky outcrops, or disturbed ground near ports where it may have been introduced. It prefers well-drained, alkaline soils and full sun exposure. You're most likely to encounter it in areas with European plant introductions or near historical settlements.

seasonality.spring: New silvery-green leaves emerge early, forming distinctive rosettes. The plant begins active growth as soil warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flower clusters most prominent from June through August. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed pods develop and ripen. Leaves may begin to yellow but often persist into early fall.
seasonality.winter: In milder winters, some basal leaves may persist. Dried stems and seed heads may remain visible above ground.

funFact: Despite being called a 'vetch,' this plant was once so valued for healing wounds that medieval soldiers would carry dried Kidney-Vetch in their packs as a kind of ancient first-aid kit, earning it the nickname 'woundwort.'
confusionNotes: With only 2 recorded observations in New England, you're unlikely to confuse it with anything simply because you're unlikely to see it! If you do spot yellow flower clusters, check for the distinctive silvery, kidney-shaped leaflets - most similar legumes have plain green leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - despite being called a 'vetch,' Common Kidney-Vetch belongs to a completely different genus than true vetches. It's an example of how common names can be misleading, as early botanists grouped plants by appearance rather than true relationships.
compareHints: Common Kidney-Vetch is the only member of its genus in North America, making it unique among legumes. Unlike true vetches which have tendrils and climbing habits, Kidney-Vetch forms low mats. Compared to other yellow-flowered legumes like wild indigo or bird's-foot trefoil, its silvery foliage and dense, rounded flower clusters are distinctive.
